The early life history of sharpsnout sea bream (Diplodus puntazzo) is characterized by rapid developmental transitions that are highly sensitive to thermal regime. At a water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], hatching occurs after a remarkably brief incubation period of only 1.1 days . Newly emerged individuals are diminutive, measuring approximately 0.28 cm  in total length at hatch, a size consistent with the small pelagic eggs typical of sparid fishes. The yolk-sac larva then undergoes progressive yolk utilization, during which it remains entirely lecithotrophic and dependent on endogenous reserves. When the rearing temperature is lowered to 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the period of yolk dependency lengthens considerably, and the larva reaches the point of first exogenous feeding—or age at birth, defined here as the completion of yolk-sac absorption—after approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days]. At this same temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the total length at birth reaches 0.31 centimeters [Lb = 0.31 centimeters]. This thermal modulation of early ontogeny reflects the underlying temperature dependence of embryonic metabolic rates, a phenomenon widely documented among temperate marine teleosts.

Following the transition to exogenous feeding, the pelagic larval phase of Diplodus puntazzo proceeds through several critical morphological milestones. The flexion stage, marked by the upward bending of the notochord tip and the onset of caudal fin ray ossification, prepares the larva for more efficient swimming and prey capture. Continued growth and fin differentiation culminate in larval metamorphosis, a profound body plan reorganization that encompasses the transformation from a planktonic to a benthic-oriented morphology. At a rearing temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], this larval-juvenile transition is completed after 90 days . Upon metamorphosis, the newly settled juvenile measures 3 cm  in total length, representing an order-of-magnitude increase from the hatchling size. This allometric shift during the pelagic-benthic transition is accompanied by the formation of scales and the development of the adult pigmentation pattern, signaling the individual's entry into the demersal juvenile stage, where it will begin exploiting the rocky reef and seagrass habitats typical of the species.

As the juvenile progresses toward adulthood, somatic growth continues at a substantial pace, and the species attains a relatively large maximum body size for a sparid fish inhabiting Mediterranean coastal waters. Longitudinal field surveys and otolith-based back-calculation studies indicate that the ultimate total length of Diplodus puntazzo reaches 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], a value representative of the largest individuals recorded in the wild. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of these maximum-sized adults has been documented at 2500 grams [Wwi = 2500 grams], though considerable variation exists depending on local habitat quality and prey availability. This asymptotic body mass is consistent with the species' position as a moderately large-bodied member of the genus Diplodus, and it typically requires several years of sustained feeding to achieve. Comparative analyses with congeneric species such as Diplodus vulgaris and Diplodus sargus suggest that the growth trajectory of D. puntazzo is characterized by a prolonged period of rapid mass gain during the sub-adult phase, followed by a gradual deceleration as the fish approaches its final dimensions.

Reproductive physiology in sharpsnout sea bream is tightly linked to the seasonal thermal cycle, and the species is a sequential hermaphrodite, typically functioning first as a male before transitioning to female at a larger size. During the peak spawning season at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) rose to 5% [GSI = 5%]. This value is within the range reported for other iteroparous sparids that exhibit multiple spawning events over an extended breeding season. Vitellogenesis onset in females is triggered by the warming spring temperatures, and the spawning period extends through the summer months, with individuals releasing pelagic eggs into the water column in a series of discrete batches. The energetic demands of gametogenesis and spawning are met through the mobilization of lipid reserves accumulated during the preceding period of high feeding activity.

Longevity and age-related reproductive milestones in Diplodus puntazzo have been assessed through mark-recapture programs and annulus readings from scales and otoliths. Under the thermal conditions of the Mediterranean Sea, where mean annual water temperatures average approximately 20 °C [T = 20 °C], female fish achieve their first reproduction at 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching], a timing that reflects the species' need to attain a sufficient body size and energetic reserves before committing to gamete production. The maximum lifespan documented for this species in the wild reaches 10 years [am = 10 years], a relatively extended duration that underscores its iteroparous, multiple-spawning life-history strategy and provides the species with multiple reproductive opportunities across its lifetime, a pattern that contrasts sharply with the shorter lifespans of smaller, more fecund sparids at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This longevity, combined with a moderate age at first reproduction, confirms that D. puntazzo follows a comparatively slow life-history pace among coastal sparids, allowing individuals multiple reproductive seasons over their lifetime to contribute to population recruitment.
